content: The Standard Treatment Regimen of Anti-tuberculosis Drugs for Patients with Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB) underwent modifications following the STREAM Stage 1 trial. These changes included replacing kanamycin with amikacin, based on evidence comparing the effectiveness of these two injectable agents. However, the recognition of permanent adverse effects caused by the toxicity of injectable agents has driven the development of newer treatment approaches, such as shorter, injectable-sparing regimens. The South African Department of Health provided observational data to the World Health Organization (WHO) on a 9-month, all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline. This regimen was reviewed and recommended by WHO in 2019. The recommended combination of medicines included 4–6 months of bedaquiline (Bdq), levofloxacin (Lfx) or moxifloxacin (Mfx), ethionamide (Eto), ethambutol (E), pyrazinamide (Z), high-dose isoniazid (Hh), and clofazimine (Cfz), followed by 5 months of Lfx (or Mfx), Cfz, Z, and E. In 2022, new evidence from South Africa led to a modification of this regimen, replacing 4 months of ethionamide with 2 months of linezolid (Lzd, 600 mg). MDR-TB and rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR-/RR-TB) have become significant global challenges due to poor management of drug-susceptible TB and the transmission of drug-resistant strains. While MDR-/RR-TB is treatable, it requires longer and potentially more toxic treatment regimens. Efforts to reduce treatment duration have spurred the search for shorter and safer regimens. In 2016, WHO recommended a standardized 9-month regimen containing an injectable agent, which was shorter than the existing 18–20-month standard of care for eligible patients. This recommendation was based on observational studies conducted in various Asian and African countries. In 2018, the STREAM Stage 1 trial results prompted further modifications to the shorter regimen, including the substitution of kanamycin with amikacin. The toxicity of injectable agents, which can cause permanent adverse effects, has led to the development of injectable-sparing regimens. South Africa's observational data on a 9-month, all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen was shared with WHO, which subsequently recommended it in 2019. The regimen was further refined in 2022 to include linezolid instead of ethionamide. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly impacted TB services, reversing years of progress. There was a global decline in the number of newly diagnosed and reported TB cases, with an 18% drop in 2020 compared to 2019. This decline brought the numbers back to 2012 levels, far below the approximately 10 million people who developed TB in 2020. Reduced access to TB diagnosis and treatment has led to an increase in TB-related deaths, with 1.5 million deaths in 2020, up from 1.4 million in 2019. Among HIV-positive individuals, TB deaths increased to 214,000 in 2020, up from 209,000 in 2019. The number of people receiving treatment for drug-resistant TB also decreased by 15% between 2019 and 2020, with only 150,359 people enrolled in treatment in 2020. This represents about one-third of those in need. Despite these challenges, treatment success rates for MDR-/RR-TB have improved globally, reaching 59% in 2018, compared to 50% in 2012. Drug-resistant TB remains a global challenge, with treatment regimens often being long, toxic, and expensive. There is a critical need for more effective and shorter treatment regimens to improve outcomes, minimize adverse events, and prevent the development of additional drug resistance. WHO's consolidated guidelines on drug-resistant TB treatment, updated in 2022, reflect these priorities. Two observational studies compared the 9-month regimen with linezolid (used in South Africa in 2019) and the 9-month regimen with ethionamide (used in South Africa in 2017). Both datasets were obtained from programmatic settings in South Africa. Adverse events were reported in 5% of participants receiving the linezolid regimen, but no direct comparisons could be made due to the lack of data for the ethionamide regimen. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) judged the benefits of the linezolid regimen to be small and the undesirable effects to be moderate compared to the ethionamide regimen. The certainty of evidence was judged to be very low. Linezolid is associated with adverse effects such as myelosuppression (manifesting as decreased platelet levels, white blood cell counts, or anemia), optic and peripheral neuropathy (which may be irreversible), and lactic acidosis. Patients experiencing recurrent nausea, vomiting, unexplained acidosis, or low bicarbonate levels while on linezolid should undergo immediate medical evaluation, including a lactic acid blood test. Ethionamide, on the other hand, is associated with gastrointestinal upset, anorexia, hepatotoxicity, endocrine effects (e.g., gynecomastia, hair loss, acne, impotence, menstrual irregularities, and reversible hypothyroidism), and neurotoxicity. Patients taking ethionamide should receive high doses of vitamin B6 to mitigate neurotoxic effects. Potential biases in the observational data include misclassification of relapse and death, as well as limited information on baseline disease severity. The findings may not be generalizable to other populations, as the studies were conducted in South Africa, a country with a high prevalence of HIV. Additionally, drug susceptibility testing for second-line drugs was not routinely performed, leading to potentially inaccurate estimates of amplified drug resistance. The GDG considered the shorter duration of linezolid and the avoidance of ethionamide in balancing the benefits and harms of the regimens. However, the certainty of evidence remains very low, and further research is needed to optimize treatment strategies for drug-resistant TB.
